title: MemeCap: A Dataset for Captioning and Interpreting Memes (Hwang and Shwartz, EMNLP 2023)
rule: A meme's meaning is a visual metaphor plus the post context; interpret the situation it maps onto, do not describe the picture or copy its on-image text.
example: 30 sampled memes: models trailed human captions by 36.6 (correctness), 29.3 (textual completeness), 24.5 (visual completeness) and 18.4 (faithfulness) points. MiniGPT4 BLEU fell 8.2 without the post title.
llm_tell: Reads visuals too literally, fails the metaphor, copies text from inside the meme, hallucinates (fine-tuned model more so). Models of 2023 era (OpenFlamingo-9B, MiniGPT4); may not hold for current models.

title: Wu, Weber, Mueller, IUI 2025: humans vs LLM vs human-AI meme creation
rule: Fixed, classic templates plus a topic make LLM output rate well on average; the best individual memes are still human-made, so the ceiling is human. LLM help raised idea count and not quality.
example: 150 per condition; GPT-4o given a 10-word image description and told to write 20 captions per topic; crowd raters scored funny/creative/shareable. AI-only highest mean; humans took most top-4 humour slots; human-AI half of top shareability. Work-topic memes drove the gaps.
llm_tell: Mean-good, never the best: competent on stock templates (Doge, Fry style) with a safe relatable topic (work); no outliers. Single session, crowd raters, summary figures only (no means in text).

title: AI generates memes funnier on average, but humans are funniest (press release)
rule: Quoted authors: more output from human-AI teams does not mean better output.
example: "The increased productivity of human-AI teams does not lead to better results, just to more results." People using AI felt less ownership.

title: The problem with brands chasing memes
rule: Do not use a format you cannot say the reason it is funny for; the format may be funny because of who uses it. Speed matters: a late post is worse than none. Keep a consistent voice first so a trend does not force a new personality.
example: "How do you do, fellow kids" as the standard failure; a brand sounding like someone handed a list of words they may use; Aldi UK 'Super 7' drew comments that the meme was already over; Duolingo's years-built Duo persona and Ryanair's long-standing self-deprecation fit trends without strain.
llm_tell: Copies the surface (slang, template) without the reason it is funny; arrives after the trend; the voice changes per trend. Marketing blog, not research.

title: same page: explaining and commercial motive
rule: Never label the joke or the relatability. A caption like 'we're being so relatable' or #relatable kills the subtext; keep the post short and slightly detached. (Search-summary paraphrase of a social media writer cited in results; original not opened.)
example: Captions such as 'We're being so relatable!'
llm_tell: Announces the joke; sells at the end; the audience sees the sales intent once the brand joins.

title: Know Your Meme: Nobody
rule: A phrasal template has a fixed frame and an open slot: opener ('Nobody:', 'No one:', 'Literally no one:') then the unprovoked, specific, recognisable behaviour; 'Me:' flips it to self-description. The joke is the contrast between nobody asking and the thing done.
example: Earliest tweets about 1 Sept 2018; sub-formats followed in weeks (J.K. Rowling parodies from 17 Nov 2018, emoji-art road crossings Feb 2019, TikTok effect May 2019). Page gives no explicit quality criteria; the 'what works' reading is an inference from the examples.
llm_tell: Fills the slot with a generic behaviour that anyone might do (nothing specific to recognise), or explains after the colon line.

title: Paper on Know Your Meme's snowclone category (via search result)
rule: Know Your Meme defines snowclones by the user's ability to change part of the phrase for comic effect; some entries fix the phrase and some leave a single slot open. A format is an agreement about what stays fixed and what varies.
example: 'IDK I've Never' (Feb 2020: wrong guesses at a title's plot), 'Nobody Will Remember' (parody of inspirational posts, humorous attribute in the slot), 'If Nobody Got Me, I Know God Got Me' (exploitable image).

title: Shifman, Memes in Digital Culture: content, form, stance (search summaries of the 2014 book and JCMC article)
rule: A meme is a set of items sharing content, form and/or stance, made aware of one another, and copied and altered by many users. A new item must show awareness of its siblings. Stance is the author's attitude toward the content, from earnest to ironic distance.
example: Form = visual/audible makeup and genre conventions; content = ideas; stance = ironic distance or earnest advocacy. Book not opened; from abstracts and reviews.
llm_tell: Writes an isolated joke with no awareness of the format's siblings, and picks the stance (sincere vs ironic) at random.

title: Milner, The World Made Meme (blurb only)
rule: Five logics of memetic media: multimodality, reappropriation, resonance, collectivism, spread. New items are built from familiar material and collectively transformed. Publisher blurb only; book not opened.

title: Computational Humor with Multimodal LLMs: survey (2026, via search snippet)
rule: Multimodal humour needs non-literal meaning, shared cultural knowledge and communicative intent, which is where models fail.
example: PixelHumor: top models 61% on panel sequencing of 2,800 comics, below humans. PunMemeCN: VLMs struggle with homophone puns even with chain-of-thought.
llm_tell: Cultural reference and wordplay across modalities are weakest. The 'stale template' link is the searcher's inference, not stated by sources.

title: Her Campus / Tartu / Melbourne pieces on layers of irony (search result snippets)
rule: Common framing: sincere, ironic, post-ironic (starts sincere, goes through irony, returns to the point), meta-ironic. Post-irony is where earnest and ironic intent cannot be separated; the reader must be in on it. Sources are student and journalism pieces plus one revised-quadrant paper; none opened. No measured claim.
llm_tell: A model picks one flat irony layer and states it; it cannot hold the earnest-and-ironic ambiguity.
